title: A sample is only as good as its coverage: reading space-filling designs, dominance and propagated spread
summary: Three figures about what to do with samples: compare how evenly three samplers fill a box, extract the non-dominated points from a two-objective sample, and push input uncertainty through a response to see the output histogram. Each asks what the points are, not what the optimiser did.

media.alt: Three square scatter plots of points in a unit box, titled monte-carlo, sobol and latin-hypercube, each showing a centre-L2 discrepancy. The monte-carlo panel, 0.004263, shows visible clusters and gaps. The sobol panel, 4.101e-05, is the most even. The latin-hypercube panel, 0.0002506, is in between.

source.caption: Sampler coverage — plain random vs. two quasi-Monte-Carlo designs
group: 08_08_sampler_comparison: three samplers on the 2-D unit box with the centre-L2 discrepancy printed above each panel (representative)
09_09_pareto_zdt1: 300 random points from the ZDT1 two-objective problem, the non-dominated subset in red joined by a line, and the true reference front in grey
13_13_uq_propagation_histogram: a histogram of a Rosenbrock response under Normal input uncertainty, with the mean and the plus/minus one standard deviation band marked
source.note: The input distribution parameters and sample size for the propagation figure are not stated on the figure.

read_the_figure.question: Do the points fill the space evenly, which of them are not beaten on every objective, and how wide is the output spread caused by input uncertainty?
read_the_figure.axes: Sampler figure: both axes are the unit interval (x1 and x2); three panels, same number of points. Pareto figure: x is objective f1 (0 to 1), y is objective f2 (0 to about 7); both are minimised, so lower-left is better. Histogram figure: x is the propagated response value (0 to about 500), y is the count in each bin.
look_at: Sampler panels: look for clusters and empty holes. Plain Monte Carlo has both; the quasi-random designs spread points more evenly.
The number above each sampler panel (discrepancy) is the single-number summary of that evenness: smaller is more even.
Pareto figure: a red point is on the front if no other point is at least as good in both coordinates. Grey points are dominated; the grey curve is the true front for the problem.
Histogram: the tall bar next to zero and the long right tail say the response is strongly skewed.
Compare the red mean line with the tallest bar: they are far apart, a sign that mean and mode differ in a skewed distribution.
read_the_figure.proves: That, at this sample size and in two dimensions, the quasi-random designs fill the box more evenly; that the extraction step finds the non-dominated subset of a given sample; and that the propagated output is skewed with a long tail.
if_wrong: A discrepancy printed without a stated sample size and dimension: it cannot be compared with other figures.
A front that lies far above the true front is usually the sample's fault, not the extraction's: random samples rarely land on a front.

A band mean plus/minus one standard deviation that goes below the physical minimum of the quantity (here the band starts below zero for a non-negative response) is a poor summary of a skewed distribution.
must_check: The same number of points in each sampler panel, and a stated seed.
Which direction is better on each objective axis, and whether both are minimised.
A true front or reference shown, as here, so the gap is visible.
The histogram states the number of samples and the input distribution; neither is on this figure.
Bin width and axis range, since the right tail is sparse.
as_drawn: Printed centre-L2 discrepancies: Monte Carlo 0.004263, Sobol 4.101e-05, Latin hypercube 0.0002506. Ratios: Monte Carlo is about 104 times the Sobol value and about 17 times the Latin-hypercube value (computed). The project caption says roughly two orders of magnitude for the quasi-random designs; that is true of Sobol and closer to 1.2 orders for Latin hypercube.

Pareto: five red points joined by a line, from about (0.005, 2.8) to (0.92, 0.8) (read by eye). The grey true front runs from (0, 1) to (1, 0). The red front sits above it throughout, by roughly 0.8 or more.

Histogram: mean 33.87 and standard deviation 41.94 (legend). The band mean minus one standard deviation is therefore -8.07 (computed), below zero, though the response cannot be negative. The tallest bar is near 1,670 counts in the first bin; the tail reaches about 250.

terms.meaning: Independent random points. The error of an average falls as one over the square root of the sample size, whatever the dimension.
A deterministic low-discrepancy sequence designed to fill the space evenly, with better error rates than random for smooth integrands.
A design that places exactly one point in each of n equal slices of every coordinate; it is random within that constraint.
A numerical measure of how far a point set is from uniform. Lower means more even coverage.
Point a dominates b if a is no worse on every objective and strictly better on at least one.
The set of non-dominated points: no objective can be improved without making another worse.
A standard two-objective test problem. Its true front is f2 = 1 - sqrt(f1), reached only when an auxiliary variable is zero.
Sampling uncertain inputs from a distribution, running each through the model, and describing the distribution of the outputs.

remember: Lower discrepancy means more even coverage, not more randomness.
A point is on the Pareto front if nothing beats it on every objective at once.
A front extracted from a random sample sits above the true front; extraction does not improve a sample.
Skewed outputs: report quantiles, not only mean plus/minus standard deviation.
Monte Carlo error shrinks as one over the square root of N.

understand.title: What discrepancy measures
understand.text: It compares the fraction of points that fall in a box with the volume of that box, over many boxes. A perfectly even set gives equal numbers; clusters and holes give mismatches, which show up as a larger value.

understand.title: Why the extracted front lies above the true one
understand.text: The true ZDT1 front needs an auxiliary variable to be exactly zero, which random points almost never hit. So every sampled point has a worse second objective than the front at the same first objective.

steps.title: Dominance for minimisation
steps.tex: \mathbf a\prec\mathbf b\iff \forall k:\ f_k(\mathbf a)\le f_k(\mathbf b)\ \text{and}\ \exists k:\ f_k(\mathbf a)<f_k(\mathbf b)
steps.note: The Pareto front is the set of points that no other point dominates. The red points in the figure pass this test within the sample; the grey ones fail it.

steps.title: The ZDT1 reference front
steps.note: With the auxiliary term g equal to one, the second objective is one minus the square root of the first, a convex curve from (0, 1) to (1, 0): the grey line. Sampled points have g above one, which lifts them.

steps.title: Monte Carlo error falls as one over root N
steps.note: Quadrupling the sample halves the standard error of a mean, in any dimension. It is why a Monte Carlo histogram needs thousands of runs for a stable tail.

steps.title: Why quasi-random designs can do better
steps.note: The Koksma-Hlawka inequality bounds the integration error by the variation of the function times the star discrepancy of the points. Lower discrepancy therefore lowers the bound, for functions of bounded variation.

steps.title: Mean and standard deviation of a skewed output
steps.note: For this histogram, 33.87 - 41.94 is below zero, yet the response cannot be negative. The band is a symmetric summary of an asymmetric distribution and overstates the lower spread.

worked.title: How much better is the Sobol design?
worked.problem: The printed discrepancies are 0.004263 for Monte Carlo, 4.101e-05 for Sobol and 0.0002506 for Latin hypercube. How many decades below Monte Carlo is each?

solution.text: Take the base-10 logarithm of each ratio to Monte Carlo.

worked.answer: Sobol is about two decades lower and Latin hypercube about 1.2 decades lower. 'Roughly two orders of magnitude' is accurate for Sobol only.

analyze.q: The extracted Pareto front has only five points out of 300. What does that tell you about random sampling for multi-objective problems?
analyze.hint: Most of the box is dominated.

analyze.q: The histogram band mean minus one standard deviation is negative for a non-negative response. What would you plot instead?
analyze.hint: Quantiles, or the whole empirical distribution function.

analyze.q: Latin hypercube has one point per slice of each axis yet still shows visible gaps. Why can slice-wise balance coexist with two-dimensional gaps?
analyze.hint: Balance is imposed along each axis separately, not jointly.

evaluate.q: Is a discrepancy value alone enough to choose a sampler for a surrogate model? What else matters?
evaluate.hint: Dimension, smoothness of the response, scrambling, reproducibility.

evaluate.q: The caption says solution mapping extracts a front but does not generate a good sample. Is the figure clear about that limit? How would you make it clearer?
evaluate.hint: Annotate the gap to the true front.

create: Redraw the histogram with the median and the 5th and 95th percentiles instead of a mean and a symmetric band, and add the sample size to the title.
Design a figure that shows the discrepancy of each sampler as the sample size grows, on log-log axes, with the one-over-root-N slope for random sampling drawn as a reference.

checks.q: What does a lower centre-L2 discrepancy mean?
checks.answer: The points fill the box more evenly: fewer clusters and holes relative to a uniform distribution.

checks.q: A Monte Carlo mean uses 100 samples. How many samples are needed to halve its standard error?
checks.answer: Four times as many: 400, since the standard error scales as one over the square root of N.

checks.q: Point A has (f1, f2) = (0.2, 3) and point B has (0.4, 2). Does either dominate the other?
checks.hint: Compare each coordinate; both are minimised.
checks.answer: No. A is better on f1 and worse on f2, so neither dominates; both can be on the front.

checks.q: Why is mean plus/minus standard deviation a poor summary of the histogram?
checks.hint: Skew and a physical lower bound.
checks.answer: The distribution is strongly skewed with a lower bound at zero. The symmetric band extends below zero, where the response cannot be, and hides the long upper tail.

checks.q: How would you show that the extracted front improves when the sample is larger?
checks.hint: Repeat with growing N and draw the true front.
checks.answer: Extract the front for N of 100, 1,000 and 10,000, plot all three over the true front, and report the largest vertical gap to the true front for each.
